title: Feature Engineering and Representation
subtopics: Representing real-world concepts as model inputs
learning_outcomes: Explain feature Engineering and Representation and connect at least two of its listed subtopics.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study feature Engineering and Representation within Data Fundamentals and Preparation. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Data quality and governance shape downstream outcomes. Record where data came from, what it means, and how it was transformed before training.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Features encode useful aspects of raw records for a model. Transformations should preserve meaning, avoid target leakage, and be computed the same way during training and inference.

items.text: Encoding maps categories to numerical representations a model can process. Define behavior for unseen or missing categories and fit data-dependent encoders without using the final test set.

items.title: Feature leakage
items.text: Leakage occurs when training or model selection uses information unavailable at the intended prediction time or information from evaluation data. It can produce deceptively strong offline results.

rows = [{"id": 1, "score": 8}, {"id": 2, "score": None}, {"id": 2, "score": 6}]
seen = set()
clean = []
for row in rows:
    if row["id"] in seen or row["score"] is None:
        continue
    seen.add(row["id"])
    clean.append(row)
print("kept rows:", len(clean))

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: If the output differs, check indentation and spelling, confirm you saved the intended file, and compare each input value with the example. If the example runs as expected, do not infer that it proves a trained model works; this snippet is a deterministic teaching aid. Keep sensitive data out of tests.

content_blocks.title: Check before you trust a result
content_blocks.text: This is a small, deterministic teaching example—not a trained AI model or evidence of production performance. Run it with a local Python 3 interpreter; do not paste secrets or private data into experiments.

content.task: Try it yourself: create six synthetic records for feature engineering and representation. Identify a quality issue, document a repeatable handling rule, and show how the rule changes the data without leaking test-set information.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core concept and accurately refer to the source syllabus topics.

hints: Write down the inputs, expected output, and assumptions before changing the example.
Change only one input or condition and compare the results with your original prediction.
Ask whether the example covers realistic cases, important subgroups, and failure conditions; a toy example does not establish production reliability.
troubleshooting: Use Python 3 and run the file from the folder where it was saved.

If Python reports a syntax error, check copied quotation marks, indentation, and whether the full code block was copied.
